content: Group B Streptococcus (GBS), also known as Streptococcus agalactiae, is a gram-positive bacterium commonly found in the gastrointestinal and genital tracts of humans. Approximately 13% of pregnant women are colonized with GBS, though colonization rates may be higher in certain subgroups. While GBS colonization is typically harmless in the general population, its presence during pregnancy increases the risk of maternal peripartum infections, preterm premature rupture of membranes, and preterm birth. Newborns can acquire GBS infection through aspiration of infected amniotic fluid or contact with the bacteria during delivery. About 40–50% of infants born to GBS-colonized mothers will themselves become colonized. GBS infection in newborns is associated with significant perinatal morbidity and mortality. It is a leading cause of severe neonatal infections, affecting over 390,000 newborns annually. In 2020, GBS infection was estimated to cause approximately 46,200 stillbirths and up to 91,900 infant deaths. Additionally, 37,100 children who survived invasive GBS infections were predicted to develop moderate or severe neurodevelopmental impairments. Early-onset GBS (EOGBS) disease, defined as the presence of GBS in a newborn’s blood, cerebrospinal fluid, or other sterile sites within the first seven days of life, is the leading cause of early-onset neonatal sepsis. EOGBS can be prevented through intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (IAP), which involves administering antibiotics to pregnant women during labor. The World Health Organization (WHO) currently recommends IAP for women with GBS colonization to prevent early neonatal GBS infection. However, the recommendation does not specify methods for determining GBS colonization or assessing the risk of EOGBS based on other factors. Given the severe consequences of EOGBS for newborns and families, as well as ongoing debates and variations in screening practices, it is essential to evaluate the effectiveness of maternal screening strategies in preventing EOGBS and improving maternal and neonatal outcomes. Maternal screening strategies aim to assess the risk of EOGBS infection either by identifying maternal GBS colonization or by evaluating maternal risk factors associated with EOGBS. These strategies help identify women eligible for IAP, thereby reducing the transmission of GBS from mother to newborn. It is important to note that EOGBS can still occur even when maternal GBS cultures are negative. Potential approaches for assessing EOGBS risk include: 1. Universal Screening: All pregnant women undergo antepartum culture-based screening (using rectovaginal swabs) to detect GBS colonization. IAP is administered to those with evidence of colonization. 2. Risk Factor-Based Screening: IAP is administered to pregnant women with one or more risk factors for EOGBS infection, without performing swabbing for GBS colonization. 3. Combined Strategy: A combination of universal screening and risk factor-based screening. 4. No Specific Screening Strategy: IAP is administered based on individual clinical assessments. Risk factors commonly considered in the risk-based approach include maternal fever, rupture of membranes, bacteriuria, and a history of a previous child with EOGBS. These factors may vary across different settings. Regardless of the strategy, most pregnant women with known GBS bacteriuria (e.g., detected through urine testing for urinary tract infections) or a history of a previous child affected by EOGBS will receive IAP. When determining the most effective method for reducing EOGBS disease, contextual factors such as local GBS prevalence, country income levels, rising antimicrobial resistance, and potential associations between early antibiotic exposure and altered gut microbiome, asthma, or obesity should be considered. The WHO has established a systematic process for prioritizing the development of maternal and perinatal health recommendations. This process is overseen by an international group of independent experts, the Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG), which identifies maternal and perinatal health recommendations in urgent need of development. The GSG prioritized the development of a WHO recommendation on screening pregnant women for IAP to prevent EOGBS disease in newborns. This complements the existing WHO recommendation supporting IAP for women with GBS colonization. The recommendation was developed in accordance with the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development, which includes synthesizing available research evidence, using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) methodology, and formulating recommendations through a Guideline Development Group (GDG) composed of international experts and stakeholders. The primary aim of this recommendation is to improve the quality of care and outcomes for women and newborns by preventing EOGBS disease. The target audience for this recommendation includes health professionals responsible for developing national and local healthcare guidelines and protocols, particularly those related to the prevention and treatment of peripartum infections. This includes midwives, nurses, general medical practitioners, obstetricians, maternal and child health program managers, and relevant staff in ministries of health and training institutions. The recommendation is also relevant to women giving birth, professional societies involved in maternal care, non-governmental organizations promoting people-centered maternal care, and implementers of maternal and perinatal health programs. The term “woman” in this context includes individuals who have given birth, even if they do not identify as women or mothers. It is recognized that some individuals who have given birth identify as gender diverse. This recommendation specifically addresses GBS screening strategies to determine eligibility for IAP in women at or near term. Vaccination, intrapartum rapid testing, and other methods to reduce GBS infection that are not currently feasible in healthcare settings are beyond the scope of this recommendation. Two key questions guided the development of the recommendation: 1. Among pregnant women at or near term, does a screening strategy for IAP to prevent EOGBS disease in newborns, compared with no screening strategy, improve maternal and neonatal outcomes? 2. Among pregnant women at or near term, does a screening strategy for IAP to prevent EOGBS disease in newborns, compared with another screening strategy, improve maternal and neonatal outcomes? The population affected by this recommendation includes all pregnant women at or near term and their newborns.
